title: Basic Safety for Water and Wastewater Operators
audience: Operators and trainees across the US and Canada preparing for certification exams and renewal in water and wastewater work.
prerequisites: Basic familiarity with plants, pump stations and distribution or collection work. This course teaches recognition and purpose and does not replace site training; your facility procedures, permits and the rules that apply to you govern. US customary units are primary with metric equivalents; all scenarios and facility data are fictional.
introduction: Learn to find hazards before work starts and to choose the strongest control: the hierarchy of controls, PPE, labels and safety data sheets, confined space and atmosphere awareness, trench, traffic, energy and lifting hazards, and chemical and emergency awareness. Each module ends with a fictional scenario and checks that name the mistake behind each wrong answer.
delivery: Self-paced lessons, optional quick checks, a graded final exam and a non-credit certificate. Duration is being validated; no contact-hour award is made.

modules.title: Hazard recognition and personal protective equipment
objectives: Find hazards before work and rank controls using the hierarchy of controls.
Match PPE to the hazard it protects against and read labels and safety data sheets.
Recognise respirator program, falling-object, abrasive blasting, solvent and biological hazards and their basic controls.
modules.lesson: ### Start with the hazard, not the injury Most injuries at a plant, pump station or collection site come from ordinary hazards nobody stopped to name: a wet floor, an unguarded belt, an unlabelled drum, a hose across a walkway. A **hazard** is anything with the potential to cause harm: a chemical, a moving part, a height, a noise, an energized wire. **Risk** is the combination of how bad the harm could be and how likely it is. > **Your job:** before any task, ask what could hurt someone, how bad and how likely, and what the strongest control is. ### Finding hazards before work A job hazard review is a short look at a task: walk the area, then think through each step and ask what could go wrong. Useful prompts are **energy** (can anything start, move, fall or discharge?), **substances** (what is present, and is it labelled?), **environment** (weather, noise, traffic, low-lying areas) and **people and time** (alone, at night, in a hurry, new to the task?). Many sites rank hazards with a matrix. This fictional scale scores severity 1 to 5 and likelihood 1 to 5, then multiplies. **Worked example.** At the fictional Cedarline pump station, a crew lists two hazards. A worn stair tread is a slip risk: severity 3, likelihood 4. A missing guard on a belt drive could cause a serious injury if someone reaches in: severity 5, likelihood 2. - Stair tread: 3 x 4 = **12** - Belt guard: 5 x 2 = **10** Both need action, and the stair tread ranks first because it is more likely. Ranking sets the order of fixes, not what to ignore: until the guard is back, the drive is kept stopped or out of reach, because a score never makes an exposed moving part acceptable. Adding instead of multiplying is a common mistake: it makes different hazards look equal (3 + 4 = 7 and 5 + 2 = 7). ### The hierarchy of controls Once a hazard is found, choose a control. Controls are ranked from most to least effective because higher ones do not depend on a person remembering every time. 1. **Eliminate** the hazard: move a valve to ground level and nobody needs a ladder. 2. **Substitute** something safer, such as a water-based cleaner in place of a solvent. 3. **Engineering controls** isolate people from the hazard: guards, enclosures, ventilation, railings, interlocks and sound housings. 4. **Administrative controls** change how work is done: procedures, training, signs, permits and schedules. They depend on people following them. 5. **Personal protective equipment (PPE)** protects the person when the hazard remains. It is the last line of defence because it removes nothing and relies on correct selection, fit, condition and use. Move up the list whenever you can. Ear muffs in a loud room protect one person, but enclosing the noisy equipment protects everyone who walks in. ### Personal protective equipment: what protects what PPE is chosen for the hazard found in the review, not by habit. | PPE | Protects against | Common mistake | | --- | --- | --- | | Hard hat | Falling objects, overhead bumps | Wearing a cracked or old shell | | Safety glasses, goggles, face shield | Flying particles, splashes, spray | Using plain safety glasses where a chemical splash is possible | | Hearing protection | Noise damage over time | Wearing it loosely or removing it for a short task | | Respirator | Dust, vapors or gases in the air, matched to the cartridge | Using the wrong cartridge or skipping the fit check | | Gloves | Cuts, heat, chemicals, biological material | Wearing a glove type that the chemical passes through | | Safety boots | Crushing, punctures, slips, chemicals | Soft-soled shoes near heavy loads | | Fall protection | Falls from height | Anchoring to something not rated for the load | PPE must suit the hazard, fit you and be inspected before use. A glove that suits one chemical may fail within minutes against another, so the SDS and your facility procedure decide. Head, eye, hearing and foot protection come in grades: a hard hat that resists impact may not resist electrical contact, goggles that seal against splash differ from open-sided glasses, and a safety boot may add toe or sole protection that a work shoe lacks. Read the rating marks and match them to the review. **Respirators** need a program, not just a mask. The wearer is medically cleared to wear one and, for a tight-fitting respirator, is fit tested on the model and size in use and checks the seal each time it is put on. Facial hair or a loose strap can break the seal. An air-purifying respirator filters the air around you with cartridges chosen for the contaminant. It makes no oxygen, so it does not replace knowing what is in the air; module 2 returns to this. ### Hazard communication: labels and safety data sheets Hazard communication means nobody handles a product without knowing what it can do. Two tools carry the information: the container label and the safety data sheet (SDS). A **label** gives a quick warning at the point of use: product name, supplier, signal word, hazard statements, precautionary statements and pictograms. A flame marks fire hazards, most often a flammable product; corrosion means the product can burn skin or eyes or damage metal; a gas cylinder means gas under pressure; and a skull and crossbones means acute toxicity that can kill or poison in small amounts. The hazard statements beside a pictogram say which hazard applies. An **SDS** carries the full detail in a standard set of sections. Know what each is for: - **Identification** names the product, the supplier and an emergency contact. - **Hazard identification** gives the hazards, pictograms and signal word. - **Handling and storage** says what to keep the product away from. - **First-aid measures** covers exposure until medical help arrives. - **Exposure controls and personal protection** lists engineering controls and suited PPE. - **Stability and reactivity** says what the product reacts with. - **Toxicological information** describes health effects. Properties, disposal and transport sections fill in the rest. The label is the first look and the SDS the full reference, so keep SDS copies within quick reach. An unlabelled container is an unknown hazard: do not open, smell, mix or pour it, keep others away and report it. Label any smaller container you fill. ### Housekeeping, falling objects and storage Housekeeping is a hazard control. Wet floors, hoses across walkways, loose cords, cluttered stairs and poor lighting cause slips, trips and falls, among the most common injuries here. Good housekeeping finds the cause, not just the puddle. A drip from a pump seal wets the floor again within the hour, so the strong control is to fix or report the leak, with cleaning and marking as interim steps. Route hoses and cords overhead or cover them, keep handrails in place and report burned-out lights. Things fall too. Anything on a platform, catwalk or landing can drop onto a person below, which is why those edges carry a **toe-board**, a low solid strip that stops tools and debris sliding off. Under overhead work the area below is marked and kept clear, and hard hats are worn. Store materials so they cannot topple: heavy items low, stable stacks, bags and drums on pallets, aisles open to exits and extinguishers. ### Dust, abrasive blasting, paint and solvents **Abrasive blasting**, often called sandblasting, drives grit at high speed to strip paint and rust from steel. Rebounding grit and dust harm lungs and eyes, and old coatings may hold toxic metals. It is specialist work: the blaster wears a hood with supplied air, the area is fenced and the hose is controlled so it cannot whip. Recognise it, keep clear, and ask whether a safer method can replace it. **Paints, coatings and solvents** give off vapors that irritate, intoxicate or burn. Read the label and SDS, keep containers closed, ventilate, and remove ignition sources. Solvent-soaked rags go in a closed metal can. A tank interior is usually a confined space, and coating vapors can add a hazardous atmosphere, so the confined-space program and its permit decide how the work proceeds. ### Biological hazards and hygiene Wastewater, sludge and some raw water carry bacteria, viruses and parasites, and animals and insects add bites and stings. Wash hands with soap and water after handling anything contaminated and before eating, drinking or smoking. Cover cuts, keep food out of work areas and change out of soiled clothing. Follow your health program on vaccinations such as tetanus. After a bite or sting, clean the wound, report it and get medical advice. ### Working alone Many operators work alone on nights, weekends and at remote sites. A person who slips and cannot call out may lie unfound for hours. Controls are mostly administrative: a check-in schedule with a named contact, a working phone or radio, a plan for a missed check-in and limits on tasks that need a second person. A check-in does not make a risky task safe; it limits how long a problem goes unnoticed. ### Before you move on You can now rank controls, match PPE to its hazard, read a label and find the right SDS section. Module 2 applies this to confined spaces.

### Fictional scenario: the Cedarline pump station walk-through

Cedarline is a fictional pump station. During a pre-job walk-through the crew finds four things: a worn stair tread with a wet landing, a belt drive with a missing guard, an unlabelled drum beside the chemical room, and a hose stretched across the walkway to a truck. One operator will work the night shift alone.

### Your decision

For each item, name the hazard, rate severity and likelihood on a 1 to 5 scale and multiply, then pick the strongest practical control from the hierarchy and say what PPE, if any, remains necessary. Describe a check-in plan for the night operator.
modules.assignment: Prepare a one-page hazard review for the Cedarline walk-through. For each of the four items give a risk score, the control you choose and its level in the hierarchy of controls. Add the PPE you would still require and one sentence on how a label or safety data sheet would help with the unlabelled drum.
rubric: Scores each hazard by multiplying severity and likelihood and ranks them.
Chooses the strongest practical control and names its level in the hierarchy.
Matches PPE to the hazard and does not treat it as a replacement for stronger controls.
Treats the unlabelled drum as an unknown hazard to be left closed and reported.
modules.facilitatorGuide: Sample scoring on the fictional scale: stair tread 3 x 4 = 12, belt guard 5 x 2 = 10, unlabelled drum severity 4 x likelihood 2 = 8, hose 2 x 4 = 8. Strong controls: repair or replace the tread and cover the landing, restore the guard (engineering), leave the drum closed and report it, reroute the hose. Learners often add the two scores instead of multiplying or list PPE first. The night operator needs a check-in schedule with a named contact; do not accept a plan that treats check-ins as making a risky task safe.

checks.prompt: A fictional crew finds that a noisy blower can be enclosed in a sound housing so staff do not need ear protection in that room. In the hierarchy of controls, the housing is:
choices: An engineering control isolating the hazard
A PPE control that protects the worker's ears
An administrative control limiting exposure time
An elimination control that removes the blower
checks.explanation: A housing around the source is a physical barrier that works without anyone remembering to use it, which is the definition of an engineering control. The "A PPE control that protects the worker's ears" choice treated the housing as personal protection, but it works on the equipment, not on the worker. The "An administrative control limiting exposure time" choice confused a physical barrier with a rule about how long people stay in the room. The "An elimination control that removes the blower" choice assumed the hazard was removed, but the blower still runs and the noise is only contained.

checks.prompt: A fictional operator wants to know what to do if a product splashes into the eyes. Which part of the safety data sheet covers this?
choices: The disposal considerations section
The first-aid measures section
The identification section
The transport information section
checks.explanation: The first-aid section describes what to do after eye, skin, breathing or swallowing exposure until medical help arrives. The "The disposal considerations section" choice mixed up first aid with waste handling, which covers how to discard the product. The "The identification section" choice chose the section that names the product and gives contact details, which does not describe treatment. The "The transport information section" choice chose the shipping classification section, which says how the product is moved and not how to treat exposure.

checks.prompt: A fictional container label carries a flame pictogram. The hazard it most commonly signals is:
choices: A corrosive material that burns skin and metal
A gas stored under pressure in a cylinder
A flammable material that can ignite
A substance with serious toxic effects
checks.explanation: A flame pictogram signals a fire hazard, most often a flammable material; each pictogram has its own shape, so learn them as a set. The "A corrosive material that burns skin and metal" choice confused the flame with the corrosion pictogram, which shows a liquid eating a surface and a hand. The "A gas stored under pressure in a cylinder" choice confused the flame with the gas cylinder pictogram, which shows a cylinder shape. The "A substance with serious toxic effects" choice confused the flame with the skull and crossbones used for serious toxicity.

checks.prompt: A fictional operator may be splashed while transferring a liquid chemical. Which item protects the face best against a splash?
choices: Plain safety glasses with side shields
A hard hat with a wide protective brim
Cut-resistant leather work gloves
A face shield over chemical goggles
checks.explanation: Splash protection needs sealed goggles for the eyes and a shield for the face; the other items protect against different hazards. The "Plain safety glasses with side shields" choice treated impact glasses as splash protection, but liquid can run around or under them. The "A hard hat with a wide protective brim" choice assumed a brim blocks splashes, but a hard hat guards against falling objects. The "Cut-resistant leather work gloves" choice chose hand protection for a face hazard.

checks.prompt: A fictional crew at Cedarline must strip old paint from a steel tank wall by abrasive blasting. Which statement fits recognition-level safety?
choices: Blasting is specialist work with supplied air and a fenced area
Plain safety glasses and a paper dust mask give the blaster enough protection
The grit stays on the floor, so other staff can watch from the open doorway
Coating work inside a tank needs no permit because paint is not a gas
checks.explanation: Abrasive blasting throws rebounding grit and coating dust that harm the lungs and eyes, so a trained blaster uses supplied-air protection inside a fenced area. The "Plain safety glasses and a paper dust mask give the blaster enough protection" choice assumed ordinary eye and dust protection is enough, but fine dust and rebounding grit need more. The "The grit stays on the floor, so other staff can watch from the open doorway" choice ignored the dust cloud and rebound that reach bystanders. The "Coating work inside a tank needs no permit because paint is not a gas" choice forgot that a tank interior is usually a confined space and that coating vapors can add a hazardous atmosphere, which brings in the confined-space program and its permit.

checks.prompt: A fictional operator is issued a tight-fitting respirator for a dusty task. Which program step comes before the first use?
choices: Reading the filter box and picking any cartridge from the shelf
Medical clearance and a fit test on the model and size in use
A sniff test of the cartridge to confirm that it smells clean
Trimming the straps so the mask sits loose and comfortable
checks.explanation: A respirator program starts with medical clearance and a fit test, because a mask that is unsafe for the wearer or leaks at the seal gives little protection. The "Reading the filter box and picking any cartridge from the shelf" choice treated cartridges as interchangeable, but the cartridge must match the contaminant. The "A sniff test of the cartridge to confirm that it smells clean" choice used smell to judge a filter, which cannot show whether the filter works. The "Trimming the straps so the mask sits loose and comfortable" choice traded seal for comfort, since a loose mask lets unfiltered air in.

modules.title: Confined spaces and atmospheric hazards
objectives: Recognise what makes a space confined and why its air can change.
Explain the purpose of testing, ventilation, an attendant, a rescue plan and a permit, and why smell is not a warning.
Recognise what IDLH and SCBA mean and why explosion-proof equipment is required in classified flammable-gas areas.
modules.lesson: ### Why confined spaces kill Confined spaces are among the deadliest places in water and wastewater work, and many of the people who die in them are would-be rescuers. A confined space limits how fast a person can get out and how fast air can move in, so a hazard that would be minor in the open becomes severe. This module is about recognition and purpose: what makes a space confined, why its air can turn dangerous, and why each safeguard exists. It is not an entry procedure. > **Your job:** recognise a confined space, know why your senses cannot judge its air, and call trained rescuers rather than climbing in. ### What makes a space confined A space is generally treated as confined when it meets three conditions together: - It is large enough for a person to enter and do work. - It has limited or restricted ways in or out, such as a manhole, a hatch or a ladder through a small opening. - It is not designed for continuous occupancy by people. Typical examples are wet wells, manholes and vaults, sewers, digesters, clarifier and tank interiors, chemical tanks, storage reservoirs and pipe galleries. Some are **permit-required** because they have, or could have, a recognised serious hazard, such as a hazardous atmosphere, material that can engulf a person, a shape that can trap someone, or any other serious safety or health hazard. The employer evaluates spaces against the applicable rule and the program says which need a permit; do not decide on the day. Depth is not the test: a shallow vault with a small hatch can be confined, and "empty" is not "safe". ### Why the air changes The air in an enclosed space changes with what is inside, what is happening in it and what is connected to it. - **Low oxygen.** Oxygen can be used up by rusting steel, by decaying material and by combustion. It can also be pushed out by other gases such as nitrogen, carbon dioxide or methane. The danger is that a person cannot sense low oxygen. There is no smell, no taste and no warning irritation, and impairment can come on quickly. - **Hydrogen sulfide.** Sewage and sludge that go septic release hydrogen sulfide. At low levels it smells like rotten eggs. It is toxic and slightly heavier than air, so it collects low, but it also moves with air currents, so do not assume any level is free of it. - **Methane and other flammable gas.** Methane forms in digesters, sewers and sludge holding areas. It is lighter than air and tends to collect high in a space, such as under a roof or the top of a gallery. In the right mixture with air, a flammable gas can ignite from a spark, a hot surface or a static discharge. - **Chlorine.** Chlorine gas is heavier than air, irritates the eyes and lungs, and sinks to pits and trenches, entering through leaks, drains and ducts. - **Other sources.** Welding, engines near an opening (carbon monoxide) and gases from a neighbouring line. The figure is a guide, not a promise: ventilation, temperature and movement change where gases sit, so a space is tested at more than one level and again as conditions change. ### Why smell cannot be trusted "I would smell it if it were bad" has killed experienced people. First, some hazards have no smell: oxygen deficiency, carbon monoxide and sewer methane give no warning. Second, hydrogen sulfide can dull the sense of smell, so an odor that fades may mean the worker has lost the ability to detect it while the gas is still there. Third, people differ in how well they smell. The answer is instruments. A calibrated, bump-tested gas monitor reads the hazards it is designed for, and it is only as good as its calibration, sensors and reader. Know what your meter does not read. ### Why each safeguard exists Each part of a confined space program answers a specific failure that has happened to real crews. Understanding the purpose makes the rules easier to follow and harder to skip. | Safeguard | Purpose | | --- | --- | | **Atmospheric testing** | Checks the four atmosphere types (oxygen, flammable gas, toxic gas and other contaminants such as dust) before work and while it continues, because conditions change | | **Ventilation and purge** | A purge clears stale air before entry and continuous ventilation keeps fresh air moving; both support testing and do not replace it | | **Isolation of connected lines and energy** | Stops material, gas or power from entering the space while people are inside | | **Attendant, harness and lifeline** | The attendant stays outside, tracks entrants, keeps contact and summons rescue without entering; a harness and lifeline let an entrant be pulled out without a second person going in | | **Rescue plan** | Makes sure that trained rescuers and equipment are ready before anyone goes in, so rescue is quick | | **Entry permit** | Records that the hazards were identified, controls are in place, and the designated entry supervisor authorised the entry; it communicates the plan to everyone involved | A permit forces a pause in which the questions are answered before anyone is at risk. The attendant is not a lookout who can be pulled away for another job. ### Rescue awareness: do not become the second victim When a worker collapses in a space, the instinct is to rush in. Resist it. The same atmosphere or hazard that downed the first person will down the second, and often a third. Rescuers who enter without the right equipment and training are a leading reason that confined space incidents become multiple fatalities. If you see a coworker in trouble in a space, call for help and activate the rescue plan. Stay out unless you are a trained, equipped member of the rescue team, and do not rely on holding your breath. Every safeguard in the table exists so that rescue is never improvised. ### Breathing apparatus and classified areas (recognition only) A filtering respirator is a poor fit for a confined space: it supplies no oxygen and cannot handle a large or unknown contaminant. **IDLH** stands for immediately dangerous to life or health, air where a short exposure could kill, cause lasting harm or leave a person too impaired to escape. An unknown atmosphere is treated as IDLH until tested. A space that is or may be IDLH calls for **SCBA**, a self-contained breathing apparatus that carries its own air supply on the wearer's back, or an airline (supplied-air) respirator fed through a hose that also has its own escape air supply. An ordinary airline respirator without escape air is not enough, because the hose can fail. Both need medical clearance, fit testing and specific training. Rescue teams use them; an untrained operator does not pick one up in an emergency. **Explosion-proof equipment** matters where flammable gas or vapor may be present, such as a digester gallery or fuel room. The site's hazardous-location classification, set under the applicable code, marks which areas need it. An explosion-proof housing is built so that if gas inside ignites, the housing contains the blast and cools what escapes, so the surrounding atmosphere does not ignite. The name does not mean the equipment cannot fail. Check the rating mark before bringing in a light, meter, radio, drill or phone, because an ordinary one can be the spark. Intrinsically safe instruments limit their energy so they cannot ignite gas. The rating has to match the area, and unrated items are not swapped in. ### Worked example: reading a gas meter *The Alder Bend lift station is fictional. The constants below are given in the example and are not exposure limits.* Meters show different hazards in different units. Oxygen is read in percent by volume, flammable gas often as a percentage of the lower flammable limit, and toxic gases usually in parts per million (ppm). Converting between ppm and percent is common: **10,000 ppm = 1 percent by volume** At Alder Bend, a fictional meter reads 2,500 ppm for a gas. To express this in percent, divide by 10,000: 2,500 ppm / 10,000 = **0.25 percent by volume** To go the other way, multiply by 10,000. A reading of 0.3 percent is 0.3 x 10,000 = **3,000 ppm**. Direction check: ppm is a much larger number than percent, so ppm to percent should shrink the number. Remember what the number does not tell you. Whether a reading is acceptable depends on the gas and on the rule or permit that applies, never on a figure you half remember. Your job is to know what the meter is telling you and to stop and ask when it is not what you expected. ### Before you move on You can now name the features of a confined space, explain how the air becomes dangerous and what each safeguard is for. Module 3 turns to excavations, traffic, energy and lifting.

### Fictional scenario: the Alder Bend lift station

Alder Bend is a fictional town. A lift station wet well has been quiet for a week. A technician plans to enter to free a float switch. The operator who last visited noticed a faint rotten-egg smell that was gone by the end of the visit. A coworker suggests that a quick look is enough because the pump is off and the smell has cleared. The fictional meter reads 3,000 ppm for one gas.

### Your decision

Explain why the plan should not proceed as described, name the hazards that may be present and where each would collect, convert the meter reading to percent by volume, and state what each safeguard in a permit program is for.
modules.assignment: Write a half-page memo for the Alder Bend crew. Explain why the wet well is treated as a permit-required space, why smell cannot be trusted, and what role the attendant, the rescue plan and the permit each play. Convert 3,000 ppm to percent by volume and show the unit conversion.
rubric: Identifies the space as confined and explains why its air may have changed.
Explains why the faded smell is not evidence that the gas has cleared.
States the purpose of testing, ventilation, attendant, rescue plan and permit without describing entry steps.
Converts 3,000 ppm to 0.3 percent by volume with the correct direction and units.
modules.facilitatorGuide: 3,000 ppm / 10,000 = 0.3 percent by volume. Key points: the space may hold gas or low oxygen after a week; hydrogen sulfide can dull the sense of smell; methane collects high and heavier gases collect low; ventilation supports testing and does not replace it; the attendant stays outside; the rescue plan exists before entry; nobody enters to rescue unless trained and equipped. Reject answers that give an entry procedure, quote an acceptable gas limit from memory, or rely on the pump being off as protection.

checks.prompt: A fictional supervisor asks what makes a space confined. Which description is closest?
choices: Lies below ground level and is reached by a fixed ladder
Holds liquid, sludge or chemical product that could be released
Can be entered, has limited exits, is not for regular occupancy
Has a hatch that locks from the outside when it is closed
checks.explanation: A space is confined when it can be entered, has restricted entry or exit, and is not designed for continuous occupancy. The "Lies below ground level and is reached by a fixed ladder" choice used depth as the test, but a shallow vault with a small hatch can be confined and a deep open pit may not be. The "Holds liquid, sludge or chemical product that could be released" choice used the contents as the test, but an empty vault can be confined. The "Has a hatch that locks from the outside when it is closed" choice chose a feature that is not part of the definition.

checks.prompt: A fictional wet well was clear on Monday. Why might it be hazardous on Friday?
choices: Air in a closed space stays the same until someone enters
Clear outdoor air means the air inside is clear too
Hazards change once the entry permit has expired
Decay, rust, leaks or nearby work can change the air
checks.explanation: The air in a space changes with its contents and connected lines: decay and leaks add gas, and rusting uses up oxygen, so an earlier clear result does not carry forward. The "Air in a closed space stays the same until someone enters" choice believed an unopened space holds a fixed atmosphere, but the contents keep reacting. The "Clear outdoor air means the air inside is clear too" choice judged the space by the air outside, but gas and low oxygen build up inside where air does not move freely. The "Hazards change once the entry permit has expired" choice treated the permit as the cause of the hazard instead of a record of it.

checks.prompt: Why is smell a poor warning for hydrogen sulfide?
choices: It can dull smell, so the odor fades while gas remains
It has no odor at any level of concentration
A weak odor means the space is probably safe to enter
Its odor depends on the temperature and humidity of the air
checks.explanation: Hydrogen sulfide can deaden the sense of smell, so a fading smell does not mean the gas has gone. The "It has no odor at any level of concentration" choice stated that it has no odor, but at low levels it smells like rotten eggs. The "A weak odor means the space is probably safe to enter" choice assumed odor strength tracks danger, but the sense of smell can be lost. The "Its odor depends on the temperature and humidity of the air" choice chose a factor that is not the cause of lost detection.

checks.prompt: What does the term IDLH describe in respiratory protection?
choices: A rating showing a cartridge filters most gases and vapors from the air
Air where brief exposure can kill, injure for life or stop escape
A permit category for work near hot surfaces or open flames
A label showing that a gas meter passed its bump test
checks.explanation: IDLH means immediately dangerous to life or health: air where a short exposure could kill, cause lasting harm or leave a person unable to escape. The "A rating showing a cartridge filters most gases and vapors from the air" choice mixed up the term with a filtering cartridge rating. The "A permit category for work near hot surfaces or open flames" choice mistook it for a hot work category. The "A label showing that a gas meter passed its bump test" choice mistook it for an instrument check label.

checks.prompt: What is the job of the attendant posted outside a permit-required space?
choices: Enter quickly when an entrant stops answering calls
Test the air once and then leave the site
Stay at the opening, track entrants, summon rescue
Keep the permit on file for the supervisor to review
checks.explanation: The attendant stays outside, keeps track of the entrants and calls rescue; the attendant does not enter. The "Enter quickly when an entrant stops answering calls" choice sent the attendant in, which can create a second victim. The "Test the air once and then leave the site" choice turned a continuing monitoring role into a single task. The "Keep the permit on file for the supervisor to review" choice treated the attendant as a clerk instead of the person who watches the entrants.

checks.prompt: A fictional operator sees a coworker collapse inside a manhole. What is the safe awareness response?
choices: Climb in at once because seconds count for rescue
Hold your breath and enter a short way in
Lower a fan, then go in to check
Call for trained rescue and stay out
checks.explanation: Untrained entry turns one victim into two; the safe response is to call for trained rescuers and keep others out. The "Climb in at once because seconds count for rescue" choice rushed in, and the same atmosphere can overcome the second person. The "Hold your breath and enter a short way in" choice believed a breath-hold protects against a hazardous atmosphere. The "Lower a fan, then go in to check" choice assumed brief ventilation makes unprepared entry safe.

modules.title: Excavations, traffic, energy and lifting
objectives: Explain why trenches collapse and what sloping, shoring and shielding are for.
Recognise the purpose of traffic control, lockout and tagout, and safe lifting, tool and noise controls.
Recognise the purpose of grounding, GFCI protection, hot work permits, arc screens and crane and hoist safeguards.
modules.lesson: ### Hazards that come from outside the building Crews work around trenches, vehicles, electricity, heavy loads and tools, and each hazard looks routine. This module covers the purpose of the controls, not step-by-step procedures; your facility program, competent person and applicable rules govern the details. > **Your job:** recognise what makes each hazard dangerous, know what protection is for and stop work when something looks wrong. ### Why trenches cave in Soil is heavy. A cubic foot weighs roughly a hundred pounds (45 kg) or more, so even a small section of wall can bury a person in seconds. Soil that looks solid can fail without warning. Usual contributors: - **Water:** rain, a high water table or a leaking pipe softens soil and adds weight. - **Vibration:** passing trucks, compactors and nearby equipment shake walls loose. - **Added load:** spoil piles, equipment and materials placed near the edge push on the wall. - **Soil type and disturbed ground:** sand, loose fill and ground near an old utility cut are unstable. Nobody enters a trench until a competent person has inspected it and protection is in place. Cracks along the edge, falling soil, bulging, seeping water and an undercut base are reasons to get out and report. ### Sloping, shoring and shielding Three common methods protect workers in an excavation, and all do the same job: keep soil from burying anyone. - **Sloping and benching** cut the trench walls back at an angle so the soil cannot slide in. Steeper walls need stronger soil; the competent person determines the angle for the soil conditions. - **Shoring** holds the walls in place with supports such as hydraulic or timber braces and boards pressed against the wall. - **Shielding** uses a prefabricated trench box or shield that stands in the trench. A shield does not hold the walls back; it protects the people inside if a wall collapses, so workers must stay within it. A competent person selects and checks the system for the soil, depth and water, and it stays until backfilling. ### Ladders, spoil piles and utilities **Means of exit.** A trench needs a safe way out within a short walk of workers, such as a ladder or ramp, so people can leave quickly if a wall fails or water rises. A ladder does not support the wall or replace trench protection. **Spoil piles and equipment.** Soil, pipe, tools and machines are kept back from the edge, where their weight pushes the wall inward and loose material can fall on workers. Keep vehicles away or use barriers or stop logs. **Buried utilities.** Before digging, utility owners mark their lines, usually through a locate service. Striking a gas, power or water line injures workers and cuts service. Marks show the approximate position of each line, not its exact path or depth, so digging near them is done with care, and a locate does not make the trench safe. ### Traffic control Roadside work puts a crew close to fast vehicles. Traffic control warns drivers early, guides them around the work area and keeps them from workers, using signs, cones, barriers, arrow boards, flaggers and lane closures. The plan is designed in advance, not improvised. High-visibility clothing is part of it, and backing trucks need a spotter. ### Electrical hazards, lockout and tagout **Shock** is current passing through the body; it can stop the heart, burn tissue and throw a person from a ladder. **Arc flash** is the intense heat and light released when current jumps through the air between conductors or to ground; the arc blast that comes with it adds a pressure wave and flying molten metal. Only qualified people work on energized equipment. Assume any wire or circuit is energized until a qualified person verifies it as de-energized. A switch that "looks off" or a machine that "is not running" is not proof. **Lockout and tagout** exist because equipment can start or release energy while someone is servicing it: electrical, hydraulic, pneumatic, gravity and stored spring or line pressure. A lock holds the energy-isolating device off, and the tag says who placed it and why. Everyone working on the equipment has a lock, and it stays until its owner removes it. Treat a lock and tag as a stop sign: do not operate it, do not remove it and do not assume it was forgotten. The steps belong to your site's energy control program and training. Carry the purpose, and the rule that no one starts, bypasses or removes a locked or tagged device. ### Grounding, cords and ground-fault protection **Grounding** (the equipment grounding conductor and bonding) gives fault current a low-resistance path back to the source, so a metal case that becomes energized trips a breaker or blows a fuse quickly instead of staying live for the next person who touches it. It reduces shock risk; it does not remove it. Do not cut off a grounding prong or use a cheater adapter. A **ground-fault circuit interrupter (GFCI)** senses a small leak of current, such as through a person, and cuts power quickly. It is the expected protection for portable tools and outlets in wet or outdoor places, and it is tested with its own button as the program directs. It limits harm; it does not make a live wire safe to touch. Extension cords are temporary. Use cords rated for the tool and for wet or outdoor use, keep them out of water and walkways, and do not chain them together, run them through doors or repair them with tape. A damaged cord or plug takes the tool out of service. ### Hot work, welding and cutting Welding, cutting and grinding throw sparks, molten metal and heat that can reach materials far from the work. Most facilities control this work with a **hot work permit** or written authorization under their hot work program. It records that the area was checked for flammable material and gas, combustibles were moved or covered, a fire watch is assigned where the program calls for one, and an extinguisher is at hand. Gas-welding cylinders and hoses are secured and kept from sparks. The arc gives off ultraviolet light that burns eyes and skin within seconds, so the welder wears a helmet with a filter lens shade matched to the process, and nearby people are shielded by **arc screens** or curtains. Fumes are controlled by ventilation or by the respirators the program specifies. Hot work near a wet well or digester is a flammable-gas hazard first, so the facility's hot work procedure and gas testing decide whether it may start. ### Lifting, ergonomics, tools and noise Back and shoulder injuries are common and cumulative. The strongest control is to remove the lift with a hoist, cart or hand truck. When a manual lift remains, clear the path, keep the load close, bend the knees, turn with the feet rather than the waist, and use a team lift for heavy or awkward loads. **Hand and power tools** cause cuts, crushing, flying particles and shock. Inspect them before use, keep guards in place, use the tool for its intended job and wear matching PPE. A defective tool goes out of service and is reported. **Noise** usually injures hearing slowly and painlessly, and a single very loud blast can harm it at once. Loudness and time both matter; the applicable rule sets the action levels and the facility's hearing program applies them. If coworkers must shout at arm's length, assume the noise needs control: enclose the equipment first, limit time next, issue hearing protection last. ### Cranes, hoists and rigging Cranes and hoists move heavy suspended loads, so routes are planned to keep loads away from people. Know the rated capacity marked on the device and on each sling, and do not exceed it. Inspect hooks, chains, slings and the hoist before use, and remove damaged items. A trained operator moves the load, a qualified rigger attaches it, and signals come from one agreed signal person, although anyone who sees danger may call a stop and the operator obeys it. Keep the load low and the path clear, and stay out from under a suspended load and out of the swing area. Keep cranes and booms away from power lines: contact can energize the machine and the ground around it. ### Worked example: a trench at Pine Hollow *Pine Hollow is a fictional town. The crew uses 1 ft = 0.3048 m.* A crew digs a trench 8 ft deep to replace a service line. Overnight rain softened the soil, a dump truck idles near the edge beside the spoil pile, and the competent person finds a crack along the edge and water seeping at the base. First, convert the depth for the metric record: 8 ft x 0.3048 m/ft = **2.44 m**. Second, list the contributors and warning signs: water-softened soil, vibration from the truck and added load from the spoil pile and truck push the wall toward failure, and the crack and seeping water warn that it may already be moving. Together they make a cave-in likely. Third, choose the response: nobody enters, the truck and spoil pile are moved back, the protective system is checked or rebuilt, and entry resumes only when the competent person approves. A ladder would not change this assessment; it is for exit, not support. ### Before you move on You can now explain why trench walls fail, why traffic control, lockout, grounding and hot work permits exist, and how to lift and rig more safely. Module 4 covers chemicals and emergency awareness.

### Fictional scenario: the Pine Hollow service line

Pine Hollow is a fictional town. A crew is replacing a service line in a trench 8 ft deep beside a driveway. It rained overnight. A dump truck idles at the edge, the spoil pile is next to the trench, and a crack runs along the surface a few feet from the wall. Nearby, a coworker has locked and tagged a pump disconnect, and another worker lifts a heavy bag of material alone.

### Your decision

Name the factors that raise the cave-in risk, say which protective methods the competent person could consider and what each does, convert the trench depth to metres with 1 ft = 0.3048 m, and explain what the lock and tag mean and what to do about the solo lift.
modules.assignment: Prepare a short field note for the Pine Hollow crew. List the cave-in factors, describe the purpose of sloping, shoring and shielding, convert the trench depth to metres, explain the purpose of the lock and tag on the disconnect, and suggest a safer way to handle the heavy bag.
rubric: Names water, vibration and added load as cave-in factors and the surface crack as a warning sign.
States the purpose of sloping, shoring and shielding and notes that a ladder is not protection.
Explains that a lock and tag mean do not operate or remove, and proposes a mechanical or team lift.
modules.facilitatorGuide: 8 ft x 0.3048 = 2.44 m. Factors: rain softening the soil, truck vibration, spoil pile and truck weight near the edge, and a surface crack signalling movement. The competent person chooses the protective system; the operator should stop work and keep out until it is approved. A lock and tag mean someone is working on the equipment, so nobody starts it or removes the lock. For the lift, use a cart, hoist or team lift. Reject answers that treat a ladder as support or a locate as protection from cave-in.

checks.prompt: Why can trench walls that look solid still collapse?
choices: Heavy soil can fail from water, vibration or added load
Dry-looking soil stays stable until someone touches it
Walls fail in sand but hold in any clay soil
Soil gets stronger under the weight of heavy equipment nearby
checks.explanation: Soil weighs a great deal, and water, vibration and added load can make a wall fail without warning. The "Dry-looking soil stays stable until someone touches it" choice judged stability by appearance, but wall failure needs no touch. The "Walls fail in sand but hold in any clay soil" choice assumed one soil type is dependable, but conditions and water change it. The "Soil gets stronger under the weight of heavy equipment nearby" choice reversed the effect, since added load pushes on the wall.

checks.prompt: Sloping, shoring and shielding share which purpose?
choices: To pump groundwater out of the excavation
To protect trench workers from a cave-in
To keep buried utilities from being struck
To keep passing traffic away from the edge
checks.explanation: All three methods keep soil from burying a worker; they differ in how they do it. The "To pump groundwater out of the excavation" choice confused protection from soil with dewatering. The "To keep buried utilities from being struck" choice confused trench protection with locating buried lines. The "To keep passing traffic away from the edge" choice confused trench protection with traffic control.

checks.prompt: Why are spoil piles and equipment kept back from a trench edge?
choices: They make the trench look smaller to passing drivers
The soil near the edge is needed for the first backfill
Their weight can push in the wall or drop material
Setback keeps the soil near the edge from drying out
checks.explanation: Weight near the edge loads the wall and material can roll in, so piles and machines are set back. The "They make the trench look smaller to passing drivers" choice chose a visibility reason that does not address cave-in. The "The soil near the edge is needed for the first backfill" choice chose a work-sequence reason instead of a safety one. The "Setback keeps the soil near the edge from drying out" choice chose a soil-moisture reason that does not apply.

checks.prompt: What is the main purpose of traffic control at a roadside work zone?
choices: To stop traffic on the road until work ends
To mark the site for delivery drivers
To make high-visibility clothing unnecessary for crews
To warn drivers early and guide them past workers
checks.explanation: Traffic control warns, guides and separates; it supplements high-visibility clothing and does not replace it. The "To stop traffic on the road until work ends" choice treated a full closure as the general purpose; some jobs do close a road, but the usual aim is to warn drivers and guide them safely past the work. The "To mark the site for delivery drivers" choice treated the devices as site signage for deliveries. The "To make high-visibility clothing unnecessary for crews" choice believed devices replace personal visibility, but they work together.

checks.prompt: What is the purpose of lockout and tagout?
choices: To keep equipment from starting or releasing energy
To record maintenance hours for the equipment history
To warn operators that the equipment is due for service
To let a switch be turned off and on quickly
checks.explanation: A lock holds the energy-isolating device off and the tag warns who placed it, so no one starts the machine; stored energy is also released or blocked so it cannot reach a worker. The "To record maintenance hours for the equipment history" choice treated the lock as a record-keeping device. The "To warn operators that the equipment is due for service" choice treated the tag as a service reminder. The "To let a switch be turned off and on quickly" choice treated it as a convenience for quick restarts.

checks.prompt: What is the safest assumption about a wire or circuit before it has been verified as de-energized?
choices: It is dead if the switch handle looks off
It is live and can shock or cause an arc
It is dead if the equipment is not running
It is harmless if the insulation looks intact
checks.explanation: Appearance does not prove isolation, so treat a circuit as live until a qualified person verifies it is not. The "It is dead if the switch handle looks off" choice trusted the appearance of a switch, which can be wrong or backfed. The "It is dead if the equipment is not running" choice assumed idle equipment is safe, but the circuit can still be live. The "It is harmless if the insulation looks intact" choice assumed intact insulation guarantees no hazard.

modules.title: Chemical safety and emergency awareness
objectives: Recognise common treatment chemicals, their hazards and why incompatible products are stored apart.
Describe awareness-level responses to leaks, spills, fire and emergencies, and the roles of drills, near-miss reports and security.
Recognise hydrogen peroxide, cross-connection and non-potable marking, battery, food and laboratory contamination and fire-class hazards.
modules.lesson: ### Chemicals do useful work and can hurt you Operators handle disinfectants, pH adjusters, coagulants, fluoride compounds and polymer daily. Each is dangerous when mixed, spilled or mistaken for something else. This module teaches recognition and awareness; handling and emergency procedures belong to your facility's plans and training. > **Your job:** know what each chemical can do, keep incompatible products apart, spot leaks early and respond through the plan. ### Common treatment chemicals and what to recognise | Chemical | What it is used for | What to recognise | | --- | --- | --- | | **Chlorine gas** | Disinfection | Greenish-yellow gas, sharp odor, heavier than air, harms eyes and lungs; liquid under pressure in cylinders and ton containers | | **Sodium hypochlorite** | Disinfection | Corrosive bleach solution; loses strength with age, heat and light; releases chlorine gas with acid | | **Ammonia** | Chloramine disinfection | Pungent gas or solution; irritates eyes and lungs; reacts with chlorine products to form harmful vapors | | **Caustic soda** | pH and alkalinity adjustment | Strongly corrosive to skin, eyes and some metals; releases heat when diluted | | **Acids** | pH adjustment, cleaning, scale removal | Corrosive; reactions with other products can release gas or heat | | **Hydrogen peroxide** | Oxidizing, odor control and some cleaning uses | Strong oxidizer; concentrated liquid burns skin and eyes; contamination can break it down, releasing oxygen and heat that burst a sealed container, so it is stored vented, away from fuels; flush contact with water at once | | **Polymer** | Coagulation and dewatering aid | Spilled polymer is extremely slippery when wet; dust or mist can irritate | | **Fluoride compounds** | Fluoridation | Dust and concentrated solutions are toxic and irritating; follow the SDS | For each chemical ask what it can do to a person, what it reacts with and what the SDS requires. If you cannot answer, read the SDS first. ### Why incompatible chemicals are stored apart Some pairs of chemicals produce gas, heat or fire when they meet, and the meeting usually happens by accident: a leak, a forklift, a wrong hose or a pail on the wrong shelf. - **Hypochlorite and acid:** mixing releases chlorine gas. - **Hypochlorite or chlorine and ammonia:** mixing forms chloramine compounds, which are irritating and toxic vapors. - **Acid and caustic:** mixing releases a large amount of heat and can spatter violently. - **Oxidizers and fuels or oils:** can ignite or speed a fire. The control is separation by design: separate rooms or secured areas, secondary containment such as curbs or trays, dedicated fill lines with connections that do not fit the wrong tank, and clear labels. Delivery is a high-risk moment, because a driver connecting to the wrong fill line can mix products. ### Cylinders, batteries and containers A damaged valve can turn a compressed gas cylinder into a leak or a projectile. Keep cylinders secured in the position the supplier specifies, which is upright for most cylinders while chlorine ton containers lie on their sides on rated supports, with valve caps or other valve protection on when not connected, move them on the right cart, keep them out of heat and report a damaged valve or smell of gas. A **regulator** steps cylinder pressure down to the working level and is made for one gas family, so nothing is borrowed from another gas, and oil or grease near oxygen fittings can ignite. Repairs are for trained people. **Batteries** differ by type. Lead-acid and some other batteries hold acid or caustic electrolyte and can give off hydrogen while charging: keep sparks away, charge in ventilated areas, wear splash protection and keep metal tools off the terminals, where a short circuit burns and spatters. Lithium-ion batteries have different hazards, mainly overheating and fire, so follow the maker's charging and storage instructions. ### Cross-connections and marking of non-potable piping A **cross-connection** is any link between drinking water and a source that could contaminate it, such as a hose left in a chemical tank or a feed line tied to process water. Reverse flow into the clean pipe is called **backflow**. It happens by **backsiphonage**, when supply pressure drops and the contaminant is drawn backward, or by **backpressure**, when the connected source is at higher pressure than the drinking water and pushes into it. Controls include an air gap, a backflow preventer tested on the program's schedule, and hoses kept out of containers. **Non-potable piping** such as reclaimed water, process water and chemical lines is marked with labels, colour bands, flow arrows and do-not-drink signs so that nobody mistakes it for drinking water. Colours and wording are set by the applicable code and your site, so learn your facility's scheme. ### Food, drink and laboratory contamination Chemicals and pathogens reach the mouth through hands, food and drink. Eat, drink and store food in designated clean areas, not in the lab, chemical room or on a bench, and keep food out of any refrigerator that holds samples or reagents. In the lab, label every bottle, do not pipette by mouth, keep containers capped, use a fume hood for volatile or corrosive work, send reagent waste through the lab's waste plan rather than the sink, and do not taste or sniff a sample to identify it. ### Recognising a spill or leak, and who to notify Early signs of a leak are damp patches, crusting around fittings, a change in odor, corroded metal, a hiss, visible vapor, a tank level drop with no matching feed or a sensor alarm. Treat a stain around a fitting as a leak that has not finished growing. The awareness-level response is short: move away, warn others nearby and notify the supervisor or the emergency contact in your plan. Trained, equipped responders manage a release; an operator who is not does not walk in to stop it. Know your escape route. The rules that apply to your site set whether a release is reportable, so know who makes that call. ### First aid awareness, eyewash and showers First aid in a chemical incident is about time, because many chemicals keep injuring tissue until they are removed. The **eyewash station and safety shower** flush a chemical from the eyes or body immediately while help is called. They dilute and remove the chemical rather than neutralize it. They must be reachable without obstruction and tested on the facility's schedule. Contaminated clothing is removed, and the SDS and facility plan say how long to flush and when a dry powder is brushed off before water is used. Know where the stations, first aid kit, SDS and emergency numbers are, and who on each shift holds current first aid and CPR training: a person who has stopped breathing needs help within minutes. Call emergency services, then follow your training and plan. Anyone exposed to a chemical should be medically assessed even if they feel better, because hydrogen sulfide and chlorine can cause delayed lung effects. ### Fire awareness Fire needs fuel, oxygen and heat, and treatment sites hold them in unusual places: digester gas, generator fuel, oxidizers near organic material and electrical equipment in damp rooms. Control **ignition sources**: no smoking, flames, sparks or unrated equipment near flammable areas, and smoke only in posted areas. Fires are grouped into classes by fuel, and an extinguisher must suit the class: ordinary combustibles such as paper and wood, flammable liquids and gases, energized electrical equipment, and combustible metals. Water on a liquid or electrical fire can spread it or shock the user, and metal fires need a special agent, so read the label. Extinguishers are for small fires, used by trained people with a clear exit. The awareness-level response follows an order: get anyone in immediate danger out if it is safe to do so, raise the alarm, close doors to contain the fire, and use an extinguisher only on a small fire with your back to the exit. If the fire is growing, leave. ### Emergency plans, drills, near misses and security An **emergency action plan** says who calls whom, where to go, who accounts for people and who talks to responders in a fire, release, medical event or storm. It helps only if people know the alarm, exits and meeting point. **Drills** test the plan under realistic conditions and find the locked door, the dead radio battery and the worker who did not know the route in a safe setting. **Near misses** are events that could have caused harm but did not: a slip without a fall, a valve left open, a small leak caught in time. Reporting them is a cheap safety tool, because the same conditions will eventually injure someone, and a report is information, not blame. **Security awareness** protects safety too. Report cut fences, unlocked chemical rooms, unfamiliar visitors and tampered locks promptly, because a gap can become a chemical or contamination hazard. ### Worked example: a cylinder at Marlowe Springs *Marlowe Springs is a fictional plant. The numbers are made up for practice.* A fictional plant feeds chlorine at a steady **12 lb/day** (5.4 kg/day) and has **96 lb** (44 kg) of net chlorine left in the cylinders on the scale. Days of supply at that feed rate: 96 lb / 12 lb/day = **8 days** The operator orders a delivery well before day 8, because rushed cylinder changes cause mistakes. Unit check: pounds divided by pounds per day gives days. Dividing the other way (12 / 96 = 0.125) gives the share of the stock used per day, not days of supply. A reviewer also finds a hypochlorite tote beside a pallet of acid. If a leak let the two mix, chlorine gas could be released, so the products belong in separate, contained areas. ### Before you move on You can now recognise the main treatment chemicals, explain why incompatible products are stored apart, and describe cross-connection, fire and emergency awareness. Your next step is to complete the checks and take the final assessment.

### Fictional scenario: the Marlowe Springs chemical room

Marlowe Springs is a fictional plant. During a weekly walk-through an operator finds a sodium hypochlorite tote on a pallet beside a pallet of acid, a damp crust around a fitting on a chemical line, a chlorine cylinder not secured, and a cut section of perimeter fence. The plant feeds 12 lb/day of chlorine and has 96 lb of net chlorine on hand. A coworker mentions that last month a worker slipped on spilled polymer and did not report it.

### Your decision

Explain what is wrong with each finding, say who should be notified, calculate the days of chlorine supply, and explain why the unreported slip matters.
modules.assignment: Write a one-page walk-through report for Marlowe Springs. For each finding give the hazard, why it matters and the awareness-level action (report, secure or move away; trained responders handle releases). Calculate the days of chlorine on hand and explain the value of the near-miss report.
rubric: Explains that hypochlorite and acid must be separated because mixing releases chlorine gas.
Classifies the crusted fitting as a leak to report and the loose cylinder and fence as hazards to secure and report.
Explains that near-miss reports reveal hazards and are not for blame.
modules.facilitatorGuide: 96 lb / 12 lb per day = 8 days. Hypochlorite and acid separation: a leak could release chlorine gas, so each needs its own contained area and fill line. The damp crust is an early leak sign to report. The cylinder should be secured upright with the cap on. The cut fence and unlocked room are security gaps to report. Polymer is very slippery, and the slip was a near miss or injury that should have been reported. Do not accept answers that send an untrained operator in to stop a leak or that give detailed emergency steps.
